title: Todd Furmanski - Making "Dragon's Descent," a Roguelike Action Game for the Atari 2600
speaker: Todd Furmanski
summary: Todd Furmanski, who usually works on large open-world games, describes making Dragon's Descent, a stripped-down roguelike action game for the Atari 2600. He discusses which roguelike qualities he kept (generated mazes, improvised interactions, multiple strategies, permadeath tension) and how the platform's two sprites, 128 bytes of RAM and limited ROM forced hard choices and an arcade-action style instead of text. He explains storing a level in 12 bytes using a two-byte random seed, ROM noise tables indexed to ramp difficulty, and a quadrant-based carving method guaranteeing navigable mazes with loops and dead ends. He frames the hardware limits as a cure for roguelike feature creep.

insights.claim: Procedural generation was originally used to save memory, as in an early Atari game (likely Pitfall!) that used a random number generator in about 128 bytes to produce 256 screens, whereas today it is used because worlds are too large to hand-author.
insights.detail: Furmanski contrasts the old constraint of too little computing power with modern simulation of cities and galaxies, where no one will place every star by hand. He wanted to return to the roots of the former.
insights.quote: originally we didn't have enough computing power to use traditional watham or intuitive design paradigms

insights.claim: In Dragon's Descent each level's treasure room offers a choice of health boost, firepower boost or points, but only one per level, which keeps the player moving forward and supports different playstyles.
insights.detail: Furmanski says players can choose to be a tank, a glass cannon, or a gem collector chasing high score, which he calls a really hard way to play. Since treasure is often how you heal, low health pushes you to reach the next level.
insights.quote: boost your health boost your firepower or get points but you can only pick one per level so that keeps you moving forward

insights.claim: Hard hardware limits like the Atari 2600's ROM and RAM prevent roguelike feature creep by forcing developers to stop expanding and make hard choices.
insights.detail: Furmanski notes roguelikes are very susceptible to feature creep. On the 2600, running out of memory, cycles or ROM means you must stop and decide, which he found an elegant way to approach a design.
insights.quote: roguelikes are very susceptible to feature creep

insights.claim: A core roguelike quality is improvisation: place actors and items in a space without scripting and let them each act, so interesting things happen, which Furmanski kept even in a minimal Atari game.
insights.detail: He also wanted generated mazes so players could not play blindfolded, and at least a couple of valid strategies rather than one tried-and-true way. On the 2600 this reduces to putting things in an empty room and letting stuff happen.
insights.quote: you put a bunch of actors and items objects in a space and everybody kinda does their own thing and awesome things happen

insights.claim: Permadeath creates a precarious power narrative, clawing up to near-demigod status and dying to one mistake, which aligns naturally with arcade design where a long session can end on one wrong move.
insights.detail: Furmanski compares it to the Atari arcade mentality of a quarter buying a few minutes or half an hour of play. Without save-reloading, the player keeps a sense of tension, choice and escalation.
insights.quote: you almost have a demigod likability and then you step on a nail and get tetanus and diet

insights.claim: Dragon's Descent abandoned text and became an arcade action game because text bitmaps consume too much of an Atari cartridge, giving up the expressive things text can do in roguelikes.
insights.detail: Furmanski notes roguelikes used text because that was what early computers had; on the 2600 a text bitmap takes a sizeable chunk of the cartridge, so he moved to arcade action.
insights.quote: I had to basically move into arcade action I think to make this experience and wouldn't be able to leverage the

insights.claim: Dragon's Descent stores an entire level in 12 bytes of RAM: 8 bytes as a 64-bit room-presence bitmap for an 8x8 grid plus 4 bytes for the entrance, exit, start and treasure rooms, all derived from a two-byte random seed.
insights.detail: The 2600 has 128 bytes of RAM, much of it used for graphics and input. The random number generator uses two separately settable 8-bit values, letting Furmanski track two seed streams.
insights.quote: the level was 12 bytes 8 were 64 bytes 64 64 bits for rooms and then 4 bytes

insights.claim: With only two hardware sprites, each Dragon's Descent room shows the player plus one other thing (key, treasure, exit or monster), so each encounter must be made interesting.
insights.detail: More sprites were possible only with flicker or beam-racing tricks. Furmanski mixes and matches enemy AI with room layouts so each room needs some simple tactical thinking.
insights.quote: two sprites the player and something else it the key beat a treasure beat the exit be it a monster

insights.claim: Dragon's Descent uses noise tables in ROM indexing ten room types, and raising the index range ramps difficulty by producing more ornate, more dangerous rooms with lethal walls.
insights.detail: Because RAM is scarce, tables live in ROM like a pre-baked noise texture. Adjusting indices gives the designer a fair amount of control over room complexity across levels.
insights.quote: using the indices I could actually increase how complicated the rooms are the walls are actually lethal to touch

insights.claim: Dragon's Descent places each important room in a different quadrant of the grid, adds a dummy room, and connects specific rooms through it (e.g. start to dummy to exit) so mazes are always navigable but have loops and dead ends.
insights.detail: Quadrants keep the entrance from being next to the exit. Furmanski calls the choice of which rooms connect the arbitrary 'art' part. Levels are big enough to get lost in but finishable in a minute or two.
insights.quote: I divide it into four quadrants to put each important room in one of each quadrant I then actually add a dummy room

insights.claim: Short, variable-difficulty generated levels create a 'potato chip' compulsion that marries arcade design with roguelike design, reinforced by more points for going deeper.
insights.detail: Furmanski says if one level is easy the next will likely be much harder. He adds carrots and sticks: deeper levels give more points, and one treasure per level is the main healing source.
insights.quote: you kind of have that potato chip type mentality kind of marrying the arcade design scheme with the roguelike design scheme

insights.claim: A generator bug made Dragon's Descent's grid effectively 7x8, but Furmanski kept it because level 1 came out as a great tutorial level with the treasure reached first.
insights.detail: He liked the resulting room clusters, the levels remained navigable, and he ported the seed generator to C and Java to preserve the same levels on later platforms.
insights.quote: level 1 is actually great because you stab the treasure first it's a great tutorial level didn't want to mess with that

insights.claim: Furmanski uses a minimal 2600 roguelike as his 'hello world' for learning new platforms, porting it to the Atari 7800, Game Boy and Apple IIe, and develops mostly in emulators with a batari-style BASIC before testing on real hardware via an SD cartridge.
insights.detail: He says if he can get it working on the 2600 he can get it working on almost anything, and porting teaches him a good amount about each platform. He aims for perfection by removing rather than adding.
insights.quote: this is almost my hello world for putting a game on to a new platform
